title: The Unfinished Canvas: Haina to Eutin by way of the Corso
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Haina (Kloster), the carpenter's son
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the village grown up around the old Cistercian abbey of Haina, a carpenter's wife bears a son on the fifteenth of February. Johann Conrad Tischbein works the abbey grounds in wood; his son will work Italy in oil. The family is already thick with painters, uncles and cousins and brothers who will hold easels in Kassel, Hamburg, Leipzig and Rome for two generations, so that the surname arrives in a room before the man does. Nothing yet marks this one out. He is the carpenter's boy, and the abbey walls are the largest thing he will see until he is fourteen.
suggested_refs: Kloster Haina, the former Cistercian abbey and the village around it

stops.name: Kassel, the uncle's easel
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: At fourteen he leaves the abbey village for Kassel and the workshop of his uncle Johann Heinrich Tischbein the Elder, court painter to the Landgrave of Hesse. Cousins and brothers copy antique casts and Dutch cabinet pictures at the same easels. Kassel hands him the rococo portrait manner he will spend twenty years shedding, and a surname that opens doors before any work of his own has earned them. He is one Tischbein among many in a city built around a gallery of other men's masterpieces.
suggested_refs: Johann Heinrich Tischbein the Elder, court painter at Kassel
The Kassel gallery of old masters

stops.name: Hamburg, the years nobody dated
stops.date_confidence: undated in sources; bracketed c. 1766-1771, the ISO date is a placeholder
stops.campa: He moves north to a second uncle, Johann Jacob Tischbein, whose Hamburg studio works in pure landscape. The training does not hold him; the German record says plainly that the field did not interest him. He crosses instead to his cousin Johann Dietrich Lilly, an art dealer, copyist and restorer of the port city, who turns him toward history painting: gods, heroes, the large subject. No source dates these years. The apprenticeship that decides what kind of painter he becomes is the part of his life nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: Johann Jacob Tischbein, Hamburg portraitist and landscapist
Johann Dietrich Lilly, Hamburg art dealer, copyist and restorer

stops.name: Amsterdam, the Holland journey without an itinerary
stops.date_confidence: contradicted: de.wikipedia gives 1771, en.wikipedia gives 1772-1773; route unrecorded, the pin is representative [R]
stops.campa: He crosses into the Dutch Republic to see in churches and guild halls the seventeenth-century pictures he has only copied from Kassel's gallery. No town on the route is recorded. The German account puts the journey in 1771 and the English in 1772, and the two cannot both be right; his elder brother made the same circuit, which may be where the record blurred. What he takes from Holland he never says in any surviving line. The pin here stands in for an itinerary that was never written.
suggested_refs: Dutch guild halls and church interiors of the 1770s, the standard German painter's circuit

stops.name: Haina, the return and the brother's commissions
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month defaulted; the city of the commissions is inferred [R]
stops.campa: He comes back through Bremen and reaches Haina in 1773, twenty-two years old, with eight years of other men's studios behind him. Between then and 1775 he works up portrait commissions alongside Johann Heinrich Tischbein the Younger, who is in fact his elder brother and who will be made Inspector of the Kassel gallery. The English source gives the span and names no city at all. Kassel is inferred from where the brother lived, not a fact anybody wrote down at the time.
suggested_refs: Johann Heinrich Tischbein the Younger (1742-1808), Inspector of the Kassel gallery from 1775

segments.name: Berlin, the First Rome, and Lavater's Zurich

stops.name: Berlin, the court and the lodge
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The Landgravine Philippine's word carries him to the Berlin court, where he sets up as a portrait painter and does well enough at it to stay. In 1778 he is received into the lodge Zur Eintracht. Berlin is the first city he enters on his own account rather than an uncle's, and the first that pays him for a face without the family workshop standing behind the price. He is twenty-six and competent, and outside the German courts that hire him nobody has heard of his name.
suggested_refs: The Berlin lodge Zur Eintracht, which received him in 1778

stops.name: Rome, the Kassel stipend and the foreigners' quarter
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the Piazza di Spagna pin is representative, no address is given in any source [R]
stops.campa: A stipend from the Kassel academy puts him in Rome at twenty-eight. He lodges in the quarter below the Trinita dei Monti where every foreign painter keeps a room and a model; no letter names his street, and the pin marks the quarter, not the door. Here the rococo learned from his uncles falls away. Antique statuary and the ruins push his line toward the severity he will keep for the rest of his life. He is looking at the Campagna eight years before anybody asks him to paint a poet sitting in it.
suggested_refs: The Piazza di Spagna quarter, lodging district of the northern artists in Rome

stops.name: Zurich, Lavater's rooms
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Money runs out and he leaves Rome for Zurich, into the rooms of Johann Caspar Lavater and the circle around the old philologist Bodmer. Lavater is reading faces as evidence of souls, and the portraitist listens. What passes between them turns Tischbein toward physiognomy as a theory rather than a knack. From Zurich the first letters go to a privy councillor in Weimar named Goethe, whom he has never seen. The correspondence will run five years before the two men stand in a room together.
suggested_refs: Johann Caspar Lavater's Zurich circle
Lavater, Physiognomische Fragmente (1775-1778), published before Tischbein arrived

stops.name: Rome, the ducal stipend and the second arrival
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Goethe speaks for him to Duke Ernst II of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg, and a hundred ducats a year brings him back over the Alps. This second Roman period is the settled one. He takes an apartment on the Corso with Friedrich Bury, Johann Georg Schutz, Johann Heinrich Lips and Heinrich Meyer, a working colony of German painters rather than a single studio, and becomes a fixture of the city. The stipend is a debt in pictures. He will not pay it, and the failure will cost him the friendship that arranged it.
suggested_refs: Duke Ernst II of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg, who paid the stipend on Goethe's recommendation

stops.name: Rome, Via del Corso 18, the lodger arrives
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; coordinates inherited byte-identical from the corpus Rome pin, goethe_full.journey.json:518-519
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of October a traveller reaches Rome calling himself the painter Johann Philipp Moller. The next day he moves into the apartment at Via del Corso 18, where Tischbein is already living. Goethe himself will later call this address the place of his second birth. For Tischbein it is the arrival of a correspondent of five years and of a patron's patron; for the man in the doorway it is the end of a flight from Karlsbad begun in secret on the third of September.
stops.quote: The strongest tie that holds me in Italy is Tischbein. I should never, even should it be my happy lot to return a second time to this beautiful land, learn so much in so short a time as I have now done in the society of this well-educated, highly refined, and most upright man who is devoted to me both body and soul.
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Letters from Switzerland and Travels in Italy, Rome, trans. A. J. W. Morrison (Bohn's Standard Library, London 1881; Project Gutenberg eBook #53205); entry undated in that text
suggested_refs: Casa di Goethe, Via del Corso 18, Rome
Tischbein, Goethe in the Roman Campagna (1786-1787)

stops.name: Rome, Monte Cavallo on the Feast of All Souls
stops.date_confidence: attested; the entry is headed 3 November 1786 and recalls the previous day's ceremony
stops.campa: Four days after the lodger settles in, the two go up to the Quirinal for the Feast of All Souls, to hear the Pope's own singers in the private chapel on Monte Cavallo. It is the first outing the diary records them making together, and it sets the pattern of the winter: the painter knows the city, the poet wants it explained, and neither is in any hurry about it. Goethe writes it down the following morning as a thing done with a friend rather than a sight seen.
stops.quote: I hastened with Tischbein to the Monte Cavallo.
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Letters from Switzerland and Travels in Italy, Rome, 3 November 1786, trans. A. J. W. Morrison (Bohn's Standard Library, London 1881; Project Gutenberg eBook #53205)
sources: Goethe, Italian Journey, Project Gutenberg eBook #53205
suggested_refs: The papal chapel on the Quirinal, Monte Cavallo

stops.name: Rome, the sketches laid out
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; coordinates inherited byte-identical from the corpus Rome pin
stops.campa: A week in, Tischbein lays out his drawings and sketches for the man sleeping down the hall. The judgement written that evening is warmer than anything his own countrymen have put on paper about him: great merit, full of high promise. It is the high point of his standing in Goethe's eyes, and it comes before a single brushstroke of the portrait exists. Everything after this is the slow work of disappointing a man who arrived already prepared to admire him.
stops.quote: Tischbein has long lived here; he is a sincere friend to me, and during his stay here always cherished the wish of being able one day to show Rome to me. Our intimacy is old by letter though new by presence.
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Letters from Switzerland and Travels in Italy, Rome, 7 November 1786, trans. A. J. W. Morrison (Bohn's Standard Library, London 1881; Project Gutenberg eBook #53205)
sources: Goethe, Italian Journey, Project Gutenberg eBook #53205
suggested_refs: Tischbein's Roman drawings and sketchbooks of 1779-1786

stops.name: Rome, the canvas stretched
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Tischbein's own letter; en.wikipedia's December 1787 is an error and is recorded as such
stops.campa: He writes to Lavater in Zurich that he has begun the portrait and will make it life size, the man seated on the ruins. That letter, dated the ninth of December, is the earliest hard evidence for the picture, and it settles a date the English literature gets wrong by a full year. The canvas is enormous, larger than anything he has attempted. A statuary is hired to make a small clay figure so the mantle can be draped and studied at leisure. The sitter will leave for the south before the winter is out.
sources: de.wikipedia.org, 'Goethe in der Campagna', citing Goethe und Lavater, Briefe und Tagebucher (Weimar 1901), p. 364
suggested_refs: Tischbein to Lavater, 9 December 1786
The draped clay model made for the mantle

stops.name: Rome, the size of life on a fallen obelisk
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: At the end of the year the sitter writes down what is being made of him. He is to be life size, wrapped in a white mantle, seated on a fallen obelisk, with the ruins of the Roman Campagna filling the ground behind. The description exists before the picture does. Everything the nineteenth century will read into that pose, the traveller at rest in a landscape of dead empire, is set out here in the plainest terms by the man being posed, who seems to find it agreeable and entirely unremarkable.
stops.quote: Latterly I have often observed Tischbein attentively regarding me; and now it appears that he has long cherished the idea of painting my portrait. His design is already settled, and the canvass stretched. I am to be drawn of the size of life, enveloped in a white mantle, and sitting on a fallen obelisk, viewing the ruins of the Campagna di Roma, which are to fill up the background of the picture.
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Letters from Switzerland and Travels in Italy, Rome, 29 December 1786, trans. A. J. W. Morrison (Bohn's Standard Library, London 1881; Project Gutenberg eBook #53205)
sources: Goethe, Italian Journey, Project Gutenberg eBook #53205
suggested_refs: Tischbein, Goethe in the Roman Campagna, Stadel Museum, Frankfurt

stops.name: Rome, the clay model in the draped mantle
stops.date_confidence: attested to the weeks before the 22 February departure; exact day not given, month day defaulted
stops.campa: Through January the canvas stands in the Corso apartment with the little draped clay figure beside it, and the picture begins to come forward out of the ground. Tischbein is working at the largest scale of his life, on a portrait nobody commissioned and nobody is paying for, of a man who will leave for the south in three weeks. The ruins behind the figure are not any single place. He assembles them, an obelisk here, a relief there, out of everything Rome has shown him since 1779.
stops.quote: The great portrait of myself which Tischbein has taken in hand begins already to stand out from the canvass. The painter has employed a clever statuary to make him a little model in clay, which is elegantly draperied with the mantle.
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Letters from Switzerland and Travels in Italy, Rome, written before the February 1787 departure for Naples, trans. A. J. W. Morrison (Bohn's Standard Library, London 1881; Project Gutenberg eBook #53205)
sources: Goethe, Italian Journey, Project Gutenberg eBook #53205
suggested_refs: The invented Campagna of the portrait, assembled from Roman sketches rather than one site

stops.name: Rome, the eye for nature and the eye for art
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of February the poet writes that the painter is coming with him to Naples, and that he counts it a piece of luck. Tischbein has an eye for nature and an eye for art both, which is exactly what a man wants in a travelling companion and exactly what makes him slow to finish anything he starts. The unfinished canvas stays on its stretcher in the Corso apartment while they pack. It will still be unfinished when both of them are dead and the picture is famous.
stops.quote: That Tischbein, who possesses as glorious an eye for nature as for art, is to accompany me on this journey, is to me the subject of great congratulation.
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Letters from Switzerland and Travels in Italy, Rome, 21 February 1787, trans. A. J. W. Morrison (Bohn's Standard Library, London 1881; Project Gutenberg eBook #53205)
sources: Goethe, Italian Journey, Project Gutenberg eBook #53205
suggested_refs: The Rome to Naples post road of 1787

stops.name: Velletri, the first stage of the southern road
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of departure
stops.campa: They leave Rome together on the twenty-second and take the old road south through the Alban Hills, the first stage ending at Velletri on its ridge above the plain. The poet keeps a diary of post-chaise stops and inn beds. The painter sketches where the road allows, gathering hill silhouettes and broken masonry, the raw material of a background he is carrying south in his head while the canvas it belongs to stays behind on the Corso, in the apartment full of painters he has left.
suggested_refs: Velletri and the Alban Hills stage of the Rome to Naples road

stops.name: Naples, the arrival under the volcano
stops.date_confidence: approximate; arrival dated to about 25 February 1787. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from goethe_full.journey.json:535-544
stops.campa: They reach Naples about the twenty-fifth. Tischbein already has contacts here and becomes the guide: a city built around a bay and a live volcano, louder and poorer than papal Rome and organised on entirely different principles. He knows what to look at and where the collections are kept. He has been telling this newcomer by letter for years that he wanted to show him Italy, and for three weeks in Naples he does exactly that, daily, with the whole city as the subject.
stops.quote: An excellent judge and drawer of animals, he had long before called my attention to a horse's head in brass in the Palace Columbrano.
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Letters from Switzerland and Travels in Italy, Naples, 7 March 1787, trans. A. J. W. Morrison (Bohn's Standard Library, London 1881; Project Gutenberg eBook #53205)
suggested_refs: The bronze horse's head of the Palazzo Colubrano, Naples

stops.name: Vesuvius, the monster turns mischievous
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for Goethe's report; Tischbein's own conduct on the slope is tradition [R]
stops.campa: Early March, the mountain intermittently throwing stones. The poet climbs toward the crater collecting specimens; the painter, by the account that survives, keeps back from the loose scree and the sulphur vents. The line Goethe sets down about him that day is one of the few in the whole Italian record where Tischbein's own temperament shows at all, and it does not flatter him. The two men are on the same slope and want different things from it. The travelling partnership has three weeks left to run.
stops.quote: Tischbein now felt more disgusted than ever with Vesuvius, as the monster, not content with being hateful, showed an inclination to become mischievous also.
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Letters from Switzerland and Travels in Italy, Naples, 6 March 1787, trans. A. J. W. Morrison (Bohn's Standard Library, London 1881; Project Gutenberg eBook #53205)
sources: Goethe, Italian Journey, Project Gutenberg eBook #53205
suggested_refs: The 1787 activity of Vesuvius, climbed repeatedly that spring

stops.name: Pompeii, the town coming out of the ash
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Goethe's March 1787 excursion is attested, Tischbein's presence is not [R]; day is a placeholder
stops.campa: Among the excursions out of Naples that spring is the dig at Pompeii, a fixed stop for any educated traveller on the bay. No source names Tischbein at the site. He is the constant companion of these weeks and the excavation lies a short ride down the coast road, so he is placed there and the placing is marked as inference. The half-cleared forum offers both men an antiquity more literal than Rome's picturesque decay: not ruins in a landscape, a town under ash.
sources: de.wikipedia.org, 'Italienische Reise' (Goethe's Naples excursions: Pompeii, Caserta, Capua, Herculaneum, Paestum)
suggested_refs: The Pompeii excavations as they stood in 1787

stops.name: Naples, Kniep engaged at the sketching board
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the nineteenth Goethe engages the young landscape draftsman Christoph Heinrich Kniep to draw for him. The reason given is generous and final: Tischbein has given three or four weeks of faithful help and cannot go on being a full-time explainer of Italy. A hired hand takes a friend's place at the sketching board. From this date the daily partnership loosens, and the man who wrote in November that he wanted to show Rome to this traveller is no longer the one showing him anything.
stops.quote: Tischbein for three or four weeks has faithfully lent me all the assistance in his power, and diligently explained to me the works both of nature and art.
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Letters from Switzerland and Travels in Italy, Naples, 19 March 1787, trans. A. J. W. Morrison (Bohn's Standard Library, London 1881; Project Gutenberg eBook #53205)
sources: Goethe, Italian Journey, Project Gutenberg eBook #53205
suggested_refs: Christoph Heinrich Kniep, engaged as Goethe's draftsman for Sicily

stops.name: Naples, the ship for Sicily
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; it.wikipedia's claim that Tischbein went on to Sicily contradicts the German and English accounts and is left open
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of March the poet sails for Sicily with Kniep. Tischbein does not go. He turns north instead, back to Rome and to the canvas standing where he left it five weeks earlier. The Italian encyclopaedia says he went on to Sicily; the German and English say he returned to Rome, and the account here follows the two against the one while printing the dissent rather than deleting it. Whatever the truth of that spring, the two men never travel together again.
suggested_refs: The Naples to Palermo packet of March 1787

stops.name: Rome, painting a sitter who is at sea
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the diary entry; Goethe was back in Rome from 7 June
stops.campa: Through the spring he works the great canvas in the Corso apartment without a sitter, from memory and from the sketches made on the southern road. The traveller comes back through Rome in June and looks at what has grown while he was gone; the entry of the twenty-seventh says the portrait is coming along happily, that the likeness is good, and that everybody likes the idea of it. It is the last recorded moment when the two men are pleased with each other over this picture.
suggested_refs: Goethe's diary entry of 27 June 1787 on the portrait in progress

stops.name: Naples, the removal for good
stops.date_confidence: attested to early July 1787, exact day not given
stops.campa: Early July he leaves Rome for good and settles in Naples, closer to the Bourbon court and the antiquarian circle than to the German colony on the Corso. The unfinished picture stays behind. He has it shipped down to him a year later, in 1788, and it stands in his Neapolitan studio for twelve years without being finished. A portrait of a Roman friendship reaches a different kingdom a year after that friendship has ended, and the man who painted it will not touch it again.
suggested_refs: The 1788 shipment of the unfinished canvas from Rome to Naples

stops.name: Rome, the Hector against David's Horatii
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1787 in Goethe's Italienische Reise; sits awkwardly against the early July removal to Naples, flagged and not resolved
stops.campa: At the French Academy's exhibition in Rome at the end of August, David's Horatii tips the balance of reputation toward the French. Goethe records the effect: Tischbein is provoked into beginning his Hector challenging Paris in Helen's presence, life size. It is the ambition of a history painter who has just been beaten at his own subject by a younger man. The report sits awkwardly against his removal to Naples in July, and no source consulted explains how he was in both places at once.
sources: de.wikipedia.org, 'Johann Heinrich Wilhelm Tischbein', quoting Goethe, Italienische Reise, Bericht vom August 1787
suggested_refs: Jacques-Louis David, Oath of the Horatii, exhibited in Rome 1785
Tischbein, Hector rebuking Paris

stops.name: Weimar, the word Hasenfuss
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of the letter
stops.campa: Three years pass and no picture reaches Gotha. The duke who pays a hundred ducats a year on Goethe's word has received nothing for it, and the man who gave the word is the one left embarrassed. On the second of March Goethe writes to Herder and calls his friend a coward, lazy, unreliable. The break is over an unpaid debt in canvas rather than over temperament or the difficulty of Italy. After it the two men do not write to each other for twenty-eight years.
sources: de.wikipedia.org, 'Johann Heinrich Wilhelm Tischbein', quoting Goethe to Herder, 2 March 1789
suggested_refs: Goethe's letter to Johann Gottfried Herder, 2 March 1789

stops.name: Naples, director of the Accademia di Belle Arti
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1789 by de.wikipedia; it.wikipedia's 1787-1788 is the outlier. The pin is the city, not the academy's later Via Costantinopoli building, which dates from 1864
stops.campa: In the autumn he is made director of the Accademia di Belle Arti at Naples, the kingdom's academy of painting, sculpture and architecture. It is the most secure position of his life and he holds it ten years, teaching Neapolitan and visiting painters and running the engraving projects out of it. The building on the Via Costantinopoli that carries the academy's name today was not put up until 1864, so the city stands as the pin here rather than any single false-precision door.
suggested_refs: The Accademia di Belle Arti di Napoli under Bourbon patronage

stops.name: Naples, the vases and the Homer plates
stops.date_confidence: the sources give only 'the 1790s'; the year is a placeholder and the frequently seen 1791 is unsupported
stops.campa: Through the decade he designs and prints etchings after motifs from antique vases, most likely for a supplementary fifth volume of Sir William Hamilton's Collection of Engravings from Ancient Vases, and draws the Iliad and the Odyssey from ancient models for the plates published as Homer nach Antiken gezeichnet. No single year is recorded for any of it. This is the scholarly work of his life, made in Naples, and it is the part of him that nobody now remembers.
stops.quote: Tischbein has a great knack of etching with a pen the shapes of gods and heroes, of the size of life, and even more. He uses very few lines, but cleverly puts in the shades with a broad pencil, so that the heads stand out roundly and nobly.
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Letters from Switzerland and Travels in Italy, Naples, trans. A. J. W. Morrison (Bohn's Standard Library, London 1881; Project Gutenberg eBook #53205); entry undated in that text
sources: Goethe, Italian Journey, Project Gutenberg eBook #53205
suggested_refs: Homer nach Antiken gezeichnet
Sir William Hamilton, Collection of Engravings from Ancient Vases

stops.name: Naples, the French come and the studio is abandoned
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1799, day defaulted
stops.campa: In January French troops enter Naples and the Parthenopean Republic is proclaimed; the Bourbon court has already sailed for Sicily. A court-appointed academy director has no standing at all under the new republic. He leaves the city that has been his home for twelve years, abandoning the post, the studio, and the unfinished portrait still standing in it. He is forty-seven and starts north into a Germany the same revolutionary wars are pulling apart around him.
suggested_refs: The Parthenopean Republic, January to June 1799

stops.name: Hanover, a way station on the northward circuit
stops.date_confidence: undated in sources; en.wikipedia lists Kassel, Hanover and Gottingen without dates. The 1801 sometimes attached here belongs to Hamburg [R]
stops.campa: He works his way north through the German courts looking for a position to replace the one the French took, and Hanover is one of the stops. Nothing comes of it. No commission and no patron are recorded, only a name on a list of towns the English source gives without any dates at all. From academy director in a Mediterranean capital to a painter of no fixed address, inside a single year. Kassel, where he learned the trade, is on the same list and did no more for him.
suggested_refs: The German court circuit of 1799-1800, undated in the sources

stops.name: Gottingen, the drawing academy for women
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1799-1801; the ISO date is a placeholder within that span
stops.campa: At Gottingen he founds a drawing academy for women, in a university town with no court to speak of and an educated public willing to pay for lessons. It is a long way down from the Accademia at Naples and a step toward what the rest of his working life will be: teaching rather than commissions. The old system of court painterships is coming apart around him, and what he builds while it goes down is a school for exactly the people that system never trained.
suggested_refs: The Gottingen drawing academy for women, founded 1799

stops.name: Hamburg, the school the Senate would not pay for
stops.date_confidence: undated in sources; the refusal can only be bracketed 1801-1808. The 1805 in circulation is invented
stops.campa: In Hamburg he draws up plans for a drawing school of his own. Young painters come to him about it, Philipp Otto Runge and Friedrich Overbeck among them. The Senate declines to fund it and the school is never built. No source gives a year for the refusal; it can only be placed somewhere between his arrival in 1801 and his departure in 1808. What the richest city in Germany would not pay for, a small Baltic duchy will offer him unasked six years later.
suggested_refs: Philipp Otto Runge and Friedrich Overbeck, who approached him over the Hamburg school

stops.name: Hamburg, the marriage to Anna Martha Koetting
stops.date_confidence: contradicted within a single source: de.wikipedia's Familie section gives 1806, its Leben section implies 1801. Not resolved
stops.campa: He marries Anna Martha Koetting in the city where he first learned the trade under an uncle nearly forty years earlier. Five daughters and a son will follow. The German article gives the marriage in one section as 1806 and implies 1801 in another, and both dates are printed here rather than choosing between them. He is in his middle fifties, without a post, living on portraits and on the reputation of a picture that almost nobody outside a few studios has ever seen.
suggested_refs: Anna Martha Koetting and the six Tischbein children

segments.name: Eutin, the Weimar of the North

stops.name: Eutin, the Prince Regent's offer
stops.date_confidence: year attested by de.wikipedia; it.wikipedia's 1809 is the outlier. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Peter I of Oldenburg, at this date Prince Regent of the duchy and not yet Grand Duke, offers him the post of court painter and gallery director, and buys his private collection of pictures outright as part of the arrangement. Tischbein is fifty-seven and accepts. Schloss Eutin is the duke's summer residence; the painter is engaged to teach drawing to the duke's sons and to whoever in local society wants lessons. It is the last position he will ever hold.
suggested_refs: Schloss Eutin, summer residence of the Oldenburg dukes

stops.name: Eutin, the garden house on the Stolbergstrasse
stops.date_confidence: the residence is attested for 1808-1829; the ISO date is a placeholder within that span
stops.campa: He does not live in the castle. He takes a garden house on the Stolbergstrasse, and it is still standing, with his name on a plaque. Twenty-one years pass here: portrait commissions, teaching, and designs for the tiles of the Niemann stove manufactory, of which forty-three whole stoves survive in the castle. Eutin is a town of a few thousand people. The man who ran the Naples academy spends the second half of his working life drawing antique motifs onto the sides of ovens.
suggested_refs: The Gartenhaus at Stolbergstrasse 8-10, Eutin, with its memorial plaque
The 43 Niemann stoves in Schloss Eutin

stops.name: Eutin, Aus meinem Leben begun
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1810 by de.wikipedia; the 1811 in circulation is off by a year. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: From 1810 he begins setting his life down on paper, working from decades of kept letters. Aus meinem Leben is the fullest account of the Roman winter that exists from his side of it, and it does not appear in print in his lifetime. It waits thirty-two years past his death for a Braunschweig publisher. The story of the picture, told by the man who painted it, is the last thing about him to reach anybody, and it arrives long after the picture stopped needing him.
suggested_refs: Tischbein, Aus meinem Leben, written from 1810, published 1861

stops.name: Eutin, the correspondence renewed
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: After twenty-eight years the letters start again. Goethe is sixty-eight and Tischbein sixty-six, and neither of them raises the Gotha debt. In 1821 they work together on a series of illustrated idylls, small sketches with text set against them, the last collaboration between the two. It is a reconciliation conducted entirely on paper across four hundred miles, by men who shared a Roman apartment for four months in 1786 and never stood in the same room after February 1787.
suggested_refs: The Tischbein and Goethe idyll sketches of 1821

stops.name: Eutin, the death of the court painter
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He dies at Eutin on the twenty-sixth of June, seventy-eight years old: court painter to a small duchy, author of an unpublished manuscript, engraver of Homer, designer of stove tiles. The great canvas has been out of his hands for thirty years and is somewhere in private German ownership. He has worked for sixty years. Of everything made in that time, the one thing the next two centuries will know him by is a picture he began on the Corso in 1786 and never finished.
suggested_refs: Eutin parish burial register, Kirchenbuch Nr. 97/1829

stops.name: Eutin, the grave on the Ploner Strasse
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the parish register; the exact position of the grave within the cemetery is approximate
stops.campa: He is buried on the thirtieth in the cemetery on the Ploner Strasse, four days after his death, the parish register entering him as number ninety-seven of the year. Whether the original stone survives or has been replaced, no reachable source says. There is no legend here of a lost or a moved or a desecrated grave, nothing of the kind that gathers around other Grand Tour figures. He stays where he was put, in a small Holstein town, and the record simply stops.
suggested_refs: The cemetery on the Ploner Strasse, Eutin

stops.name: Braunschweig, the memoir printed at last
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Thirty-two years after his death the memoir is printed at Braunschweig by C. A. Schwetschke und Sohn. Aus meinem Leben enters the world at the moment German readers are hungriest for eyewitness Goethe, and it is read closely for the four months in Rome and skimmed for everything else in it. The painter becomes, in print, exactly what he already was in fact: a source for another man's life, valuable in proportion to how close he happened to be standing.
suggested_refs: Aus meinem Leben, C. A. Schwetschke und Sohn, Braunschweig 1861

stops.name: Paris, Salle Favart, Mignon asks after the land
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of performance in the corpus file; coordinates inherited byte-identical from paul_barbier.journey.json:259-278
stops.campa: At the Salle Favart, Mignon sings Connais-tu le pays. The libretto is by Paul Barbier and Michel Carre out of Goethe's Wilhelm Meister, and Tischbein's portrait is counted among the images standing behind these scenes. A Paris audience of the Second Empire weeps at a German girl's memory of a country she was stolen from, and the picture in every head of what that country looks like is a Hessian painter's invented Campagna.
suggested_refs: Ambroise Thomas, Mignon, Opera-Comique, Salle Favart, 1866
Tischbein, Goethe in the Roman Campagna, cited in the Barbier journey

stops.name: Frankfurt, the Stadel receives the nation's Goethe
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Adele von Rothschild gives the picture to the Stadel in Frankfurt. It has come down through the Heigelin family and Carl Mayer von Rothschild since Tischbein abandoned it in Naples, and it enters a public collection fifty-eight years after the painter's death, in an empire busy making Goethe and Schiller into national property. The English literature reads the donation as an act of that nationalism. The reading is the article's, not the donor's, and it is marked as such here.
suggested_refs: Goethe in der Campagna, Stadel Museum, Frankfurt, inv. donated 1887

stops.name: Rome, Keyserling under the archetype
stops.date_confidence: inferred in the source file; coordinates inherited byte-identical from keyserling.journey.json:156-157
stops.campa: Hermann Keyserling reaches Rome and frames his own visit against this painting, naming it the archetype of the philosophical traveller. Keyserling stands where Goethe once stood, a hundred and twenty-one years later, re-enacting a pose that a Hessian carpenter's son composed out of studio props: a small clay figure in a draped mantle, and ruins assembled out of eight years of walking the city on a stipend.
suggested_refs: Keyserling's 1907 Rome stop, framed against the Tischbein portrait

stops.name: Rome, Via del Corso 18 opens as the Casa di Goethe
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The first floor at Via del Corso 18 opens as a museum on the thirtieth of May, after an earlier memorial room ran from 1973 to 1982 and closed for want of money. The apartment is bought in 1990, the floor above it in 2009, the enlarged museum inaugurated in 2012. Six men shared these rooms in the winter of 1786 and five of them were painters. The house is named for the one who was not, and it hangs a copy of the picture the other five watched being made on the far side of the wall.
suggested_refs: Casa di Goethe, Via del Corso 18, Rome, opened 30 May 1997
